utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. May we, as usual, hear the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, and may I today for the first time, Your Honours, introduce Katharina Margetts, a lawyer who has just joined our team and who is specifically designed to fill us in on German law and procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as assisted by Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic for the Defence. And we are not that powerful to have a German expert on our team, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are expert enough in this law system. Any problem with Mr. Ostojic, may I ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He promised to be here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Anything before we start?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just very briefly Your Honour, and it's because Your Honour raised the question of the motions under -- for dismissal under Rule 98 yesterday. Your Honours, the rules at the moment specify 10 pages as the maximum amount that one can write for such motions. I'm merely raising it at this stage to ask Your Honours to consider that that would be insufficient, I think, both for the Defence and for us on the facts of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Accepted. I personally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise. From my point of view it doesn't make sense at all. It facilitates the work of the parties when, for example, they have to concentrate for the purposes of ten pages only on the framework, and leaving them the search for the authorities and so on to others. I think there shouldn't be any limitation. But let's take this occasion to address the following. We discussed just before entering the courtroom this question: We should be aware, and we have this before our eyes, the schedule for the second part of the year. You are all aware that the Bench invited the parties to try to come to an agreement of the best possible solution and as soon as possible. I can't see any movement right now, but nevertheless, what we discussed is wouldn't it be appropriate to try to overcome this four weeks' motion, response, rebuttal, decision of the Tribunal, in the way of coming to an agreement between the parties on what basis, if any, we have to proceed for the Defence case, instead of wasting enormous amount of time and manpower for the purposes of these formal decisions. I wonder if it wouldn't be possible to come to an agreement here and to avoid this motion by doing so. It's only, once again, an invitation, and we just discussed it before coming in, and I took the opportunity to address it immediately. But when it should be necessary, no doubt, the page limitation should be no obstacle to writing whatever you feel necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously we're aware from the preamble to the schedule that Your Honour produced, I may say that we haven't had an opportunity really effectively since then to get together to discuss matters. Mr. Ostojic hasn't been here. And it is our intention, certainly before the Court break, to discuss matters with Defence counsel to see if there's any possibility of reaching an agreement. Obviously, we will do our best in compliance with Your Honours' wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate this very much. And whenever you need assistance by the Bench or a judge, let us know. We do everything necessary to come as soon as possible to a solution in this case because we all have to be aware that more and more in public opinion, the length of our proceedings are no longer accepted, opposed to the length of hearings in crimes with a nearly as difficult issue and difficult charges as we have them here in this case. And we have to take care that we don't lose all the confidence the international society is vesting into our work by deleting and deleting the cases even where it's not absolutely mandatory. But I appreciate your words and take them as a good signal that there might be a kind of agreement. There are several possibilities. We indicated today only one possibility at least to facilitate and expedite the proceedings. Is there anything else to be addressed by the parties before we come to today's witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are in open session, and no protective measures necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then may I ask the usher to bring in the witness of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May you -- once again, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can hear me also with the headset no problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And may we start the examination-in-chief immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, is your full name James Barnabas Burke Mayhew?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we'll see from reports that you're going to look at, are you commonly known and do you sign yourself as Barney?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I sign myself as Barney Mayhew. I'm known as Barney Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, I think as I've explained to you already, what you say will be translated so there may be a delay between some of the questions and your answers while the translation continues. I want to ask you a little bit about your background, please. Did you go to Oxford University, reading classics?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And upon leaving Oxford, did you enroll in the army, and were you in the army between September 1987 until December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for the record, were you, in fact, an officer in a regiment which I don't think exists any longer, but the 47th Royal Dragoon Guard?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's right, it's a tank regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst in the army, did you serve with a United Nations peacekeeping force in Cyprus?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then on a NATO deployment in Germany?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, I think you trained the post-independent Namibia Defence Force?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's right, the Namibia Defence force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally did you complete a tour in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left the army in --

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I'm just waiting. There's some catching up being done. Did you, in fact, through the foreign and commonwealth office join the then quite new organisation, the European Community Monitor Mission?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just tell us your reason for joining them?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I had left the army in 1991, slightly later than I expected. I expected to do three years or so. I extended because I found it very worthwhile and enjoyable. And my aim in joining the army was similar to my aim in continuing work with the EC Monitor Mission. I was interested in contributing what I could in the army to stopping wars from beginning. And I had always been interested in reconciliation since university days. And so as soon as I had left the army, about a month later, I saw the advertisement for the EC Monitor Mission, and it was quite clear to me from that day that that was what I wanted to do. So I applied that day and was sent out about two weeks later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, originally, did you go to Zagreb, arriving in early March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just tell us a little bit about how the structure of ECMM worked? What would happen in respect of reports?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: ECMM had a large number of teams at one point, I think, nearly 50 teams deployed on the ground. They reported typically every day, and at the headquarters, a small staff had to collate these reports into a single daily ECMM mission report. That was fed to the head of mission ultimately who would sign it, and out it would go to the 12 capitals of the European community at that time, plus the four other capitals whose nations -- who were contributing staff to the mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as we'll see, when you went into the field as it were, you yourself wrote reports. What, in your view, was important about the type of reports that you sent back?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: It was made very clear to us, and my training was consistent with this, that there should be a very clear distinction between verified confirmed facts that we had been able to verify ourselves and any other comments or opinions, and any comment had to be highlighted as such. So the reports were typically of a fairly military, terse brief style leaving out a great deal that perhaps people might have wished to say, but which wouldn't conform to the rule of reporting factually. Our role as a monitor mission was exactly that, to verify things, not primarily to pass on what others are saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you began in Zagreb, and was your task there to collate the field reports into the single report that would be sent out to each of the countries?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I don't recall whether I began by going to the field organ with a short spell at that job in Zagreb. But, at all events, my job at various points was between field missions to be collating these reports partly because of being a native speaker of English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you went into the field. At that stage, in March of 1992, were you part of a team monitoring the cease-fire line in the area of Pakrac and Lipik in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you operating the Croatian side of the line?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In late March of 1992, did you request a transfer to the Banja Luka office?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that granted?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before going to Banja Luka, did you go to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that in early April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you actually in Sarajevo still when the first shots were fired?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I had to go through Sarajevo because flights took us there, and it wasn't possible to cross the front line directly. So we had to go around it through Sarajevo. The idea was then to move directly north to Banja Luka, but because the first shots were fired in Sarajevo, I stayed there a few days while we did what we could about that situation. And it delayed my move north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So sometime after it were the opening salvo in Sarajevo, did you go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the ECMM team based in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: In the Hotel Bosna, in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in that team roughly?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Approximately seven monitors plus, I think, about four drivers. We used local interpreters as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your job in Banja Luka at that stage was to do what?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: We were given quite a broad definition, but it essentially fell into two main parts: The first part was to monitor the Croatian cease-fire line from the south, from the Serb-held side. And my aim in coming to the other side was to make sure that I had as balanced a view as I could have from both sides of that front line. The other part of the job was to monitor the situation in Bosnia, which was widely thought to be deteriorating, and to do what we could by finding out what was going on and by persuasion to calm the situation down and to prevent a slide towards war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so as far as that second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please a little bit slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Am I speaking too quickly?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's my fault, Mr. Mayhew, asking the question too quickly after the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, now as far as the second or other part of your job, monitoring the situation in Bosnia is concerned, what did that involve you doing?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: First we had to establish an open relationship, a contact, with leaders within the main population centres, so Banja Luka, Derventa, Prijedor were the three main ones, but elsewhere as well. We had to try Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to get an understanding of what was the situation. It was complicated, and so we had to speak to those people who we thought could give us a rounded view and no single person could do that. So we tried to speak to representatives of each community, secular and religious, and also to doublecheck what they were saying with reference to ordinary people who we might visit with no notice, at random, on the ground in a small village in town. So that was our first task, to try to understand a complex and changing situation. And our second task was to really left to our discretion, to do what we could to calm things down. And if that meant verifying that a particular rumour about an atrocity was true or false, and very often it was false, then we could report that back having seen with our own eyes that it hadn't happened, and try to get an accurate picture understood by all sides and to persuade military commanders in some cases and to -- not to fire and to help their own people to calm down. And our, of course, through all of this, essential was the task of reporting. And so we were constantly required to deliver a report, try to build that picture in the ECMM mission headquarters in Zagreb which would allow higher level diplomatic activity to be better focussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now let's deal with some of the matters you've mentioned. Rumours, you say: "verifying a picture rumour about an atrocity was true or false." How prevalent were these types of rumours of atrocity?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: This was a very major and important feature of the situation. Rumour alone was a cause of fighting and of violence. And we found really a pattern growing up in most areas that in one village or town they would hear of an atrocity carried out. In another area, the rumour would sweep around town let's say that two people had been killed by Croats, two Serbs had been killed, as an example. And so the Serb community would be furious and frightened. The rumour would go around. And quite often, they would then organise some sort of retaliation in their own town against the Croat community. And then it would later be discovered that the original rumour was false, but you now have a real atrocity that's being committed or a murder or rapes or robbery. And in the other town, they hear of that, but then they hear of it in an exaggerated form so it wasn't two or three people, but ten or 20 or a hundred. I give this as a sort of example. I can cite specific instances that remain in my memory, if that would be helpful. But you got this sort of multiplier effect, largely caused by rumour. So we saw it as a very important part of our job to go directly to the source of the rumour and find out what the truth was. And quite often something wrong had been done. But usually it was of a smaller scale, and we could report that back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, in fact, I think actually see by the interpreters having a bit of trouble. You can slow down slightly because you are speaking quite fast. You've said you could -- you said that you could give us an example. You can give us one example of what happened.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: In Derventa, I remember that we crossed the informal front line from the centre, out to the west of Derventa. So the centre was held by Muslims at the time. "Held" is too strong a word, an informal front line had grown up and people had polarised towards their own areas. The Serb military commander was now west of Derventa, and we went out to find him. And he said: "We have reliable information that there are a large number," I think it was 400 people, "held in the basement of a certain building in Derventa town. And they are being forced to give blood, so that there are blood supplies for the Muslim and Croat forces. And some -- they are at risk of dying." I can't remember if he said some had died. "And if this doesn't stop immediately, we will use all means at our disposal to attack and prevent this atrocity." And so we travelled back across the front line, and my colleagues verified, went down into the basement of that building with two minutes' warning and found that there were eight people, prisoners held there, Serb prisoners, but no sign of any more having been held and no sign that anyone had given blood in that basement. And so we were able then to go back to the Serb commander and say we have been there, with our own eyes we've checked, and this is what the story is. And that would deal with that rumour, and he would usually accept our word. But immediately there would be another one, yes, that's fine, but I now have very reliable information that. And I remember he cited another example of an enclave, a Serb residential area, predominantly Serb area within Derventa that was now surrounded and about to be attacked, and everyone would be killed. "And if something is not done about this, I will use every means at my disposal." This is a kind of language that we might hear on any side. I give this just as an example. So we would go and verify that people were in that place but they weren't being attacked and then we'd come back and then there'd be another rumour, so we fought a sort of losing battle. We couldn't keep up with the pace of rumours. And of course, we were only two or three people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot keep up with the pace of the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry for my speed. I will really try now to be slow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think just to be clear, unlike your colleague Mr. McLeod, this is the first time you have given evidence. So it's not quite the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Presumably, you were working through interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who provided the interpreters for you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: In almost all cases, it was the local authorities under the mayor of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You've spoken about the rumours and whatever. Through interpreters, were you able to get an idea of what was appearing in the media, newspapers, and television?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, we didn't pay close attention to local media because we heard from people's own mouths what they were hearing, and we were mostly interested in what real people thought. And if they had been influenced by the media, we would pick that up from our interviews with people. But it was of interest to us how the media was used, in a secondary sense. Our overall impression was that the media were used by the authorities there, and really in all parts of Croatia and Bosnia, to -- for propaganda, and that part of the aim of many of the media announcements was to frighten their own people into believing the worst stories about the other side or the other two sides, and to cause a polarisation and to believe, in a sense, that unless you separated from and possibly took up arms against the other side, they would come and kill you first. And it seemed to us that the great majority of people, ordinary people, were quite happy to live alongside each other, and had done so for many years. But within each of the main communities, there was a relatively small group of people who were determined to poison people's minds against the other side or the other two sides and to cause -- to cause this polarisation so that the small core groups's political aims could be achieved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us about the ordinary people that you were meeting. Did you also have meetings, and I want to turn now to Prijedor, with leaders of the parties in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anyone in particular that sticks out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Well, in that -- at that point, in April, May, we met with the council of the district, and in particular, the three leaders of the three main ethnic groups within the council, including the mayor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to recall now which the three political or the ethnic -- not the ethnic groups, but the political parties were?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: The SDS, the SDA, the Serb and Muslim. I actually don't recall the Croat party, but it was the main Croat party. HDZ, it must be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The leadership of those parties, what were they saying to you, individually or together?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, in our -- I think at that time we had just the one sort of full meeting in Prijedor with the council. And it fell into two parts. We requested that we could meet alone with each of the three main leaders, and we had a full meeting with the whole council also. We then gave a small press statement afterwards. Each ethnic group leader gave us their version of events, and the three versions were, of course, somewhat different. A key aim of each of the three sides was to show that their own side had behaved well, up until now, that their own side wished to continue in a peaceful and constructive democratic way, and that their own side had the right to remain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall what the leader of the SDS said in particular?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. I recall it particularly because he had an unusual view of democracy, it seemed to me. Using maps, he showed us that the Bosnian Serb part of the population in that area owned the great majority of the land, and I think it was about 75 per cent or something like that. And this was what gave them their right within the democratic structures, this gave them -- the implication was this gave them a greater right because of greater landownership, all the while admitting that the proportion of population was not the same as the proportion of land that they owned. This was an argument we had never heard before and was not familiar to us, and so it stuck particularly in my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that the proportion of the population was not the same as the proportion of land as they owned, in other words, they weren't the majority of the population?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't recall in fact the percentages within that district. We had maps which were very much widely used of the different proportions. Yes, but it was much less than the percentage of landownership, and I don't recall the percentage that it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, by and large, what level of leadership was ECMM dealing with?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: In northern Bosnia, we were dealing with mayors and below, typically. There was one occasion later where I met General Mladic who was just on a visit, and we met him. Just rather unusually, he agreed to see us. But normally, we were dealing at mayor or below, and at sort of colonel brigadier on the military side, that sort of level and below.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what role did you understand the mayor played in the area? I mean, why were they the people that you were seeing?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: At this stage, the problem was primarily a political problem. It was becoming a military problem, or became later a military problem. And so it was natural that we should go to political leaders first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were based in Banja Luka. Did you get to know the mayor of Banja Luka, Mr. Pedrag Radic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly before, as we'll hear, ECMM was pulled out in May, how often would you see Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: We would be in frequent touch with him, probably on average every two or three days. And it was his office that was facilitating our other needs such as security, interpreters. So we might be in touch with his office more or less daily on some administrative matter or other. And his office was a very short distance from our hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look, please, at a report that you prepared on a particular meeting with Mr. Radic dated the 13th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was attachment 2 to the statement. Your Honour, if Your Honours haven't got it for some reason, we have more copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The problem is we have numerous attachments to different documents. Just to find the correct one. It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours have found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, is this a report signed by you and I think another gentleman, or this is a typed copy? But Mr. Botonakis.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, is this a classic type of report that you would be sending back or was it something out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: This was an extra report, in addition to our regular daily reports, because a particular meeting had produced information that was particularly interesting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we just go through that report, we see that it was written or, rather, the date on the fax is the American style. It goes 92/4/19. But does that mean it was faxed through or however it was, on the 19th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: No, it would have been faxed through -- it would have been sent by a machine called CapSat, which is an early form of email, probably on the same day, the 13th of April, at the latest, the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what does "UTC time 92-04-19" mean? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: That is, almost certainly, a later faxing of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Once already received by headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it's addressed to RC Sarajevo. That was what?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's called regional centre Sarajevo, which was the Sarajevo regional sort of subheadquarters of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "From Banja Luka 1." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: That means team number 1 of the three, I think it was three Banja Luka teams. So it's the name of the team, which is Botonakis and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's dated the 13th of April, 1992. And we see it had headed "Serbian Republic within Bosnia and Herzegovina." Paragraph 1: "At a meeting today, the mayor of Banja Luka, Mr. Pedrag Radic, outlined his view of the Serbian Republic within Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, before we go on to look at what he said, how did this conversation come about exactly?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: We would meet with him frequently, as I mentioned, and it just happened that in a particular meeting, he came out with this vision of the future political shape of a Bosnian Serb part of Bosnia. I suspect that we had probably asked one of our normal questions: "How do you see the future evolving?" This would be a question we would often ask to political leaders of all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right let's look what he said. "His opinion seemed carefully thought out. He expects to be appointed as the vice-president of this republic soon, so his comments are worth noting, and are probably an accurate indication of SDS intentions. "2: The Serbian Republic within Bosnia and Herzegovina would consist of six parts: Semberija, and then it names the municipalities. North Bosnia. Romania. Birac, and then Bosanska Krajina, which includes -- what we see, well, various different municipalities including Prijedor, and then the next typed line is: "Parts of the Krajina region not specified." Is that what he said, that he mentioned other parts? He said there would be other parts not specified or that you missed what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: No, no it wasn't in this case that we missed what he was saying. This is part of the Krajina just outside the Bosnian border. And what he must have said is: "There would be some parts of that, but we have yet to decide which they would be." It was to make the point that it would not be limited only by the Bosnian border but would take some parts of those other Krajina sections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's over the border into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, as far as the borders show. Of course, that was a matter of dispute in Mr. Radic's mind since that was a predominantly Serb area, I think he wouldn't have called it Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then F, eastern Herzegovina, and again, the various areas, municipalities are listed. "3: The capital would be Banja Luka. The six parts would be a confederation within BiH, and the Serbian Republic would be very largely autonomous. It would retain close links with Serbia, including the use of the Serbian Dinar as its currency. "4: Once the Muslim and Croat constituent units of BiH are established, Radic foresees a small central government with responsibility for certain aspects of fiscal policy and foreign policy. Three foreign ministers would rotate taking turns to head the foreign ministry for six months at a time. Central government would have no responsibility for defence. "5: Radic was evasive when asked whether it was the plebiscite of the 9th, 10th November, 1991, which gave the authority for the Serbian Republic. He said vaguely that the Republic was a result of the wishes of Serbian people." Can I ask, Mr. Mayhew, how familiar were you with the events leading up to and after the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Because it was in November 1991, I had been briefed about it, but in a limited way. So I was aware of essentially what it had said. But not very much more. My memory is now quite dim of that plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 6: "He was asked for his opinion of the statement of principle, Brussels, 9 of March, 1992, Sarajevo 18th of March, 1992, he said it did not give enough autonomy to the constituent units. (See Section D of the statement of principles.) Again, Mr. Mayhew, if you can't remember, what was the statement of principles that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember the details. This was part of the diplomatic initiatives which I would have read at the time and we referred to in the conversation. But I don't recall the detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Seven: "Finally, he mentioned that the Serbian dominated areas in -- he mentioned that the Serbian dominated areas in the southeast of BiH, eastern Herzegovina would eventually join Montenegro." "8: A frequent theme of the mayor's remarks was that the EC strongly favoured Croatia and Slovenia. He seemed to believe this genuinely. He also suggested less strongly that there is an EC campaign against the orthodox church. This complaint has been heard often before." Now, which complaint, Mr. Mayhew, that the EC strongly favoured Croatia and Slovenia, or about the campaign against the orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: It's not clear from my text, and I don't recall which. My guess is that it probably refers to both complaints because I do remember both complaints being made frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "9: Despite his complaints, the mayor's manner was definitely friendly, and he seemed convinced of the potential usefulness of the ECMM." And then: "The Livno/Duvno situation, Mr. Radic warned that we should not be surprised if he took Croatian civilian hostages in order to exchange for Serbian civilian hostages held in Rascani, near Duvno. We warned him that the EC would view this with great concern, and that he would lose any moral advantage that he now has. We promised that ECMM teams would do what they could to help any Serb hostages, and urged him to be patient. The Belgrade press is taking a close interest in this case, as well as the local press here." Now, first, can you just very briefly tell us what was the reference to "Serb civilian hostages in Rascani?"

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, that the Bosnian Serb authorities had detained a number of Serb civilians in Rascani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was warning that you should not be surprised if he took Croatian civilian hostages. How did you react to this particular remark. We can see that you reported the warning, but did you take it seriously?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, we took it seriously. It was entirely within his power to do that. It was not unknown elsewhere in Bosnia, and later on, subsequent events showed that that was the sort of thing that could be done. So we thought it was a realistic feasible threat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Mayhew. That's that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be made an Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as S214.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went -- did you go to Prijedor during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you had already told us, because you said you had the meeting with the leaders of the parties there. Were you aware at any stage before you left in May of a takeover that had occurred in Prijedor by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were in Banja Luka itself, did you ever become aware of an incursion into Banja Luka by members of a paramilitary group styling themselves the SOS?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to explain how ECMM came to pull out of Bosnia, in brief.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: My colleague, Bertrand Borrey, who was a Belgian monitor was killed, shot in no man's land near Mostar, in May. I think you will have the date. And shortly afterwards, the head of mission decided that in view of that event, and the deteriorating security for all monitors in Bosnia, to withdraw us for consultation to Zagreb, which was a soft way of saying to evacuate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, did ECMM pull out of Bosnia completely until August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: They pulled out completely. They didn't know how long it would be that they would be absent. We all hoped that it would be for a matter of a few weeks perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just before we come on to the second visit you made to this area, during your time there, were you aware -- you've told us about rumours -- of any incidents, actual incidents, of intimidation?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: This is referring to which period?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period between the beginning of April and May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: There was a general atmosphere of intimidation, and whenever we spoke to people, we found them afraid. We found all three groups afraid, but the Muslim and Croat communities in that area the most afraid. So there could be no doubt in our mind that intimidation was happening in a widespread sense. As for specific incidents, we didn't investigate specific threats against an individual family, for example. We were tending to have to deal with much larger groups because we were concerned with the overall stability rather than pursuing individual cases. I have mentioned one or two examples in Derventa where --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I stop you for a moment. What I'm interested in is the sort of Banja Luka, Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: No, we didn't. As far as I recall, we didn't investigate any individual incidents. We heard of many stories and allegations of intimidation of families. But we didn't get to the detail of individual incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you left, were any restrictions placed on your freedom of movement throughout the area?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radic announced just a few days, very short time before we left, that he would now have to start restricting our freedom of movement, and the reason that he gave was for our own safety. This was a phrase that was often used by all three sides, and it was usually used when they wished to hide something. Of course, there were exceptions when they were genuinely concerned for our own safety. And our impression was that there might be some genuine reason in this, but there would probably also be some desire to stop us seeing some things that were going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you pulled out, and did you then go to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you remain there until August of -- well, I think you remained there after that. But were you there until you went back in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. I may have made one or two very brief missions out, of one or two days, but essentially I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now move, then to, that visit. Had it been decided that the CSCE, that is, the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, would send a mission to inspect what was described as places of detention in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that largely as a result of the London Conference that had been held in August?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that mission to inspect to be headed by a -- an English diplomat called Sir John Thomson?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was a retired diplomat by that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was ECMM requested to facilitate the mission's visit to the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because you had been there before, were you asked effectively to try and set this up and coordinate things?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so, as a result, did you obtain permission to visit Banja Luka in advance of the mission's arrival?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, though I think I remember that those advance missions were in order to prepare for our own return, and it so happened that then the CSCE mission intervened at very short notice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as we've heard, and as we can see on this, as it were, planning stage, were you joined by Charles McLeod? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that the first time that the two of you had worked together, or had you worked together before?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think it was our first field mission together, probably. We had worked together in the headquarters sometime before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you keep your own notes of conversations that you had with, first of all, Mr. Radic, and then other people, or would you be relying for the detail on the reports made by Mr. McLeod?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I haven't kept my own notes. And so for the detail of the conversation, I would rely on Mr. McLeod's reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not going to go through all the detail again. I've already dealt with that with Mr. McLeod. But I am just going to go through the various visits that were paid. Could you be handed, please, the report of a visit on the 23rd of August, 1992, to Mr. Radic, which has already been produced as S... Your Honour, Ms. Karper tells me it wasn't exhibited when Mr. McLeod gave evidence. I rather thought it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From the top of my head, I remember that we decided to take the entire notes as one exhibit. Is it included in this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may be the registry can help. The number on the first document is 00950317. We have a copy available for Mr. Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit S171.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, for clarification, is this the handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's the typed. But we've got a spare copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, Ms. Karper is quite right. When I went through it with Mr. McLeod, I only made an exhibit, I think, of the meeting with Stakic. I think the rest we went through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's right. And then additionally, we took into evidence the entire notes in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The handwritten ones, that's right. Your Honour, Ms. Karper was quite right. And effectively, in any event, I'm only going to just go through the basic meetings with this witness. But if he could have a copy of it anyhow. Has he got a -- you have, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a meeting with Mr. Radic; Mr. Zupljanin, the Banja Luka chief of police; and a representative of the army, Colonel Vukelic. Mr. Radic obviously you knew. What about the Banja Luka chief of police, Mr. Zupljanin, had you met him before?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Colonel Vukelic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All really I want to ask you about this, Mr. Mayhew, is what was the attitude of Mr. Radic to your return?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: His attitude was generally positive, but a great deal had happened since we had last met. And I think his attitude was therefore somewhat under strain. The situation was confused. The future was doubtful. He wasn't sure in his mind yet whether our return would be advantageous to him and to his community. He wanted to encourage us, but he stopped short of a firm and definite permission to return. He wanted some of his points of view to be well understood. We had been out of contact for some time, so that was natural. I think he was probably somewhat fearful for the future. Would his communities aims be realised? Would there be lasting peace soon? And I think all communities at that stage were confused and frightened, and I think he showed some of that, which is fully understandable. Is that enough of an answer for you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. All right. And then I think we'll deal without showing you the document, did you pay a second visit to Mr. Radic on the following day, again, with Mr. McLeod?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, if the document confirms that, I rely on the document for the dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move, then, please to the actual arrival of Sir John Thomson's mission. Did you and Mr. McLeod escort Sir John Thomson, first of all -- I think you came through Bosanski Gradiska, then Banja Luka, and the visit to Manjaca, and then did you go to Prijedor on the 31st of August?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without showing you the report, because I think -- unless you'd like it, Mr. Mayhew -- what do you remember just about Gradiska, if anything?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, this was our first -- our first visit of such a high level. And it was clear that the authorities wished to impress and to receive a high-level visitor in a formal and correct manner. There were soldiers standing to attention, lining the route for the last little part of the route, to the mayor's office, and we were very courteously received by the mayor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then moving, because for the purposes of this case, the visit to Banja Luka and Manjaca is not germane. But moving to the visit to Prijedor, I'd ask please that you be given what was exhibited, Mr. McLeod's report on the meeting with Dr. Stakic, which is S166.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can I just ask you this, Mr. Mayhew, first of all: How much of a recollection, an independent recollection, do you have of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Of the meeting in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I remember the occasion. My primary role was as a facilitator of the high-level mission. And so I was not negotiating directly. But I remember the main content and tone, certainly the main tone, and the main events, but not the detail within the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever met Dr. Stakic on your earlier visits to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't know. I had certainly met the leader of the Serb community or Serb party in, as I mentioned earlier. But I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And if asked, after a gap of ten years or so, do you think you would be able to recognise Dr. Stakic again?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I couldn't be certain. I could not be certain of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just - really, because we have been through the detail with Mr. McLeod - go to the conclusions of this report.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Page 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 5, thank you. We can see that it must have been actually written after the visit to Trnopolje, because it refers to it, although the meeting came before, I think. But I'm going to deal with the visit to Trnopolje in a moment. Because it states: "The version of events that led to the opening of Trnopolje that we were given by the mayor was in stark contrast to that given by the people we spoke to in the camp."

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I'm not on the right page I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's paragraph 41.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then 42, conclusion: "The authorities insist that they are acting in the best interests of all the people in their area and that they have no desire to get rid of the Muslim population. However, this just does not match what they are actually doing. Against this background, it is very hard to draw conclusions based on what is said. "43: The conclusion to be drawn from what we have seen is that the Muslim population is not wanted and is being systematically kicked out by whatever method is available." Now, what is important -- opinion? Is that a fair conclusion, Mr. Mayhew?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: In general, yes. I think I would have worded it slightly differently, particularly that last phrase. I fully agree with the phrase "the Muslim population is not wanted and is being systematically kicked out." We had seen plenty of evidence for that. If I was going to be very strict with my language, I would want to be just a little bit cautious about that phrase "by whatever method is available." The fact is that at that visit, many Muslim people were still living in their homes. And if the authorities had truly wanted whatever method, they could already have transported them to the border or taken other measures. So I would probably have replaced that phrase with something like "by whatever method they could get away with" or -- and possibly have allowed some room for a difference of opinion among the Bosnian Serb leadership. After all, not everyone was certain that 100 per cent of the Muslim population had to go. There was, I'm sure, a variety of opinion, hardliners, and less hardline. But there was a predominant aim, it seemed, to drive out at least enough of the Muslim population to be certain that the number remaining could be of no threat at all and would be fully subdued. That, I am confident of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Mayhew. The report can be taken back. Thank you. Now, can I ask you about the visit to Trnopolje. You prepared a report, I think yourself, on both your visit to Trnopolje and Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I wonder if you could now be handed that, please, which was attachment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One, I think it was. Yes, attachment one to the statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the first document, it was a covering letter addressed to a Mr. Gray in the foreign and commonwealth office saying -- from Mr. Melhuish. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Head of mission of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Saying: "Dear Charles, conditions inside Bosnian detention camps. As you know, we helped out Sir John's Thomson's CSCE mission to Banja Luka on the 30th and 31st of August by assigning two ECMM monitors to act as escorts and fixers. I subsequently asked one of them, Barney Mayhew, a British monitor, to record his impressions. I now attach the paper he has written for whatever purpose you may think fit. As was the case with an earlier report by Patrick Russell in my undated letter to Jeremy Greenstock, sent late July, we do not often have the chance of obtaining first-hand impressions of conditions in northern Bosnia. Whenever we do, we think the department should know, and you may wish to give this a wider circulation." And then if we go to the actual document that you produced, introduction -- I'm sorry, it's headed "Manjaca and Trnopolje." "Introduction: Between the 30th of August and the 2nd of September, 1992, an ECMM team visited Manjaca camp and Trnopolje Open Reception Centre at northern Bosnia twice each. We were escorting first the CSCE rapporteur mission, and then a representative of the EC presidency following the London Conference. The Bosnian Serb authorities were welcoming and determined that both places should be fully open to inspection." There is then a section on Manjaca. And if we go, then, to the next page where you deal with Trnopolje: "The Trnopolje, southeast of Prijedor," I imagine it should read centre or whatever, camp, "is described as an open reception centre. Wire fencing has been removed. Approximately 1600 male refugees, again, almost all Muslim, are held there for their own safety, according to the Bosnian Serb authorities, although some officials claim the refugees are free to leave. "However, small sandbag military guard posts on the edges of the centre face inwards. The centre is run by the local Red Cross, and has no visible internal discipline. Eyes are not downcast. The centre is located around some school buildings with some refugees sleeping inside the buildings, and the remainder living in improvised tents outside. Again, no provision has been made for winter." Just pausing for a moment, I'm going to come back to the whole visit, but when you say again, you're referring back to your part about Manjaca, I think.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, in Manjaca, the commandant had stated that no provision had been made for winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Food seems still be in short supply, although the ICRC is now supplying food. Water also seems to be insufficient, and diarrhea is again the biggest medical problem according to the centre's doctor. The trees seem not to be maintained. Excrement lies on the ground in several parts of the camp. When interviewed without witness, the refugees give the same story as those at Manjaca. A group from the nearby town of Kozarac told me that on the 24th of May, the Bosnian Serb army had shelled Kozarac with artillery for 30 hours before moving in to remove men, then women and children, then possessions from the houses. The houses were then burned. (The team visited part of Kozarac and found nearly all the houses burned. These houses were last seen by the ECMM in April, intact Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and inhabited.) "Several refugees at Trnopolje had claimed that some of their numbers had been shot and others had disappeared without explanation. Again, there is unison when asked what they want to do; to leave to anywhere other than Bosanska Krajina, Serb-held northern Bosnia." I'll deal with the next paragraph after I've asked you about Trnopolje. Now, Mr. Mayhew, if you can, let's put some flesh on to this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I remind you, we would have only five minutes, and I think it's appropriate, because it will be a longer issue, that we have a break now. The trial stands adjourned until 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Let me take the opportunity to immediately inform you on what happened this morning as regards the documents. Trial Chamber has received an internal memorandum from Judge Per Lindholm dated 17th of July 2002, subject documents in Stakic case. It reads: "Please be informed on the 17th July, 2002, at 11.00 in my office, a review of documents send from the United Nations Detention Unit to me was conducted pursuant to the order to the registry of the Tribunal to provide documents dated 5 July, 2002. "One, the persons present during the review included Judge Per Lindholm, Mr. Branko Lukic, Defence counsel for Milomir Stakic, Miss Katherine Gallagher, and Miss Sanja Matesic, who assisted with translation. The envelope was opened in the presence of myself and the Defence counsel for Milomir Stakic as instructed. Three, the envelope contained 22 documents, 20 documents contained Dr. Stakic's signature. Two documents included additional writings by Milomir Stakic. Also, 20 documents containing Dr. Stakic's signature, one document was a colour copy, and the remaining 19 documents were originals. 4, both myself and Branko Lukic examined every document. 5, both myself and Branko Lukic agreed that there were no confidential materials in the envelope, and all the documents could be sent to the Office of the Prosecutor. It was decided to include two documents that did not contain Dr. Stakic's signature (his driver's license and identity card) for completeness. "6, all documents were placed in an envelope addressed to the Office of the Prosecutor, attention Joanna Korner. I sealed the envelope in the presence of all, Branko Lukic included, and gave it to Katherine Gallagher for delivery to Ms. Joanna Korner." This document will be admitted into evidence as J8. And I hope, then, without further notice the handwriting expert can start the work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter that arises from that. I actually didn't get the documents. Ms. Gallagher left a message for me because I was in another court. I think Mr. Koumjian collected or Ms. Karper did. There is one matter that Mr. Koumjian wants to raise. I think I will finish this witness in chief before the end of today, so if Mr. Koumjian could raise it at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. So let's now proceed with the examination-in-chief of the witness before us. Thank you for your understanding. And proceed immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, remembering again, if you can, not to speak too quickly, and I'll try not to pick up straight at the end of an answer of yours. We read your report that you provided to your head of mission. Can you try and flesh out a little what you said about Trnopolje. You've described it as containing approximately 1600 male refugees. What most struck you about the camp?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: A number of things. The first is it was quite a relaxed atmosphere at that stage. We couldn't tell whether this was a recent innovation or whether this had always been the case. Some wire fencing had recently been removed, we noticed that. And that, combined with common sense, told us that the conditions as we saw them were likely to be somewhat improved from the recent past. It would be in the interests of the camp authorities to show a good face and to make sure that nothing too damaging was visible. Now, that is me using common sense to guess. It's not a fact that I can confirm. But the atmosphere was relaxed. Conditions of hygiene were poor. That was one of the strong impressions, excrement on the ground, no action being taken to clean that. People living in makeshift shelters covered with bits of cloth or plastic. This certainly can't be called adequate accommodation and no authority would consider that as adequate accommodation, except, of course, in an emergency for a night or two. This camp had been around longer. People were frightened, not truly -- not free to leave. Guns were pointing inwards from these guard posts as I referred to. And there seemed to be some freedom of movement, but within limits that we couldn't quite determine. So it was a mixed picture, but one of control but not of harsh control at that stage. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said the atmosphere was relaxed. How would you compare what you'd seen in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: The relaxed thing is the key difference with Manjaca, that people were free to mill around and walk about. They would be playing draughts or something or some sort of activity to keep themselves entertained or occupied. And they could walk around freely within the centre. And they would engage your eyes with eye contact. I was able to just to slip to one side into the corner of a building and have a quick conversation for several minutes with a group of people and get an impression of their stories. I couldn't have done that for long, but it was longer than Manjaca. Now, in Manjaca, just about everyone's eyes were held deliberately down like this. Some people, you know, would look up, but sort of briefly and quickly look down. A most unnatural way for anyone to behave. Similarly, when walking around the camp, heads all bowed, all uniformly hands behind back. And our impression was the regime would have had to have been particularly strict, at the very least, and probably very harsh to achieve that kind of human reaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, because I think we saw somewhere that it had been described as an open reception --

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- At the beginning of your report, an open reception centre. And you described that there was a machine-gun, I think, post or whatever facing inwards. Sorry, small sandbag military guard posts on the edge of the centre face inwards. What did that suggest to you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Well, it was quite clear to someone who had any military experience that the primary purpose of that post was to prevent people from leaving and to make the point unequivocally to the inhabitants that they were required to stay. This was at variance with the theme of the authorities locally, which was "they are there for their own protection and their own safety." So you would have simply reversed the orientation of these guard posts which had no view -- the one I'm particularly thinking of had no view external to the camp. It could only look inwards. So it was quite clearly not for the purposes of protection of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to have a look at some photographs that were taken during the course of this visit by the mission. I think not by you; you didn't carry a camera with you.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: No, I felt it could be compromising to my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we'll leave out the Manjaca ones because they are not relevant, if we could go to the ones that were taken at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did I understand correctly that this document we just had before us was tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, Your Honour is quite right. I don't think I have tendered. I haven't finished with the document yet. There is one more paragraph Your Honours will see. I just want to deal with the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could look at first of all the one bearing the number 00456962, and yes, if we could put that on the ELMO. If you turn to your right, you can probably see it on the screen as well. You will see the first photograph coming up. Do you remember this building?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I can't be certain it's the right building, but I see an ECMM colleague dressed in white in the front there. It looks very like the building which was at the front of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then could we go to the next one with the number 63. Now, is that -- you talked about this makeshift accommodation. Is that what you were meaning?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These sort of tents and that. Can you remember seeing any women at all there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I actually do not remember whether it was a mixed population or only male. I talked mainly or exclusively to men. I'm afraid I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. If we then could go to the next, number 64. A close-up apparently of one of these tents.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: That looks just like the accommodation I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 65.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, some accommodation was inside the building, and some was outside in these makeshift tents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this group here, the man in the middle of the group, in comparison to the rest, seems to be somewhat thinner. Can you recall, were there a number of men who were that sort of type of figure?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that there were a significant number of people there who were particularly thin, of this -- roughly of this degree of thinness. I can't remember the proportion in any way. In any case, we didn't survey the whole population. It was not just two or three. It was not sort of completely exceptional, but it was a significant proportion, and perhaps it was 5 or 10 per cent as a rough guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this: Before you went on this visit, had you seen the film, the news film, that had been made by the ITN news crew or any other television news crew earlier that month?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next one is the number 66 at the end. The cooking facilities, were there a number of people cooking in this fashion?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember there being a kitchen area. Now it's quite possible that there was a kitchen area, but I don't recall it. And I do recall a number of people cooking like this outside, which would suggest that they were not being fed from the kitchen area or not being adequately fed. I remember from my report that the ICRC was bringing food. This is a very significant fact in my opinion, given the duty on any detaining power to provide sufficient food. And in my private conversations with the ICRC, they were quite clear in their opinion that the level of food supplied, both here and in Manjaca, was woefully insufficient, well below what was needed. And as a last resort and under protest, they had agreed to supply food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the last photograph, please, number 67. Can you tell us what we're looking at here. Yes, this is a water tanker, water being brought to the camp in an orderly and correct fashion. I recall that water supplies were said to be on the low side, and I don't have accurate recollection of precisely how much water was supplied. But this is a, in my opinion, a perfectly reasonable way to supply water to a temporary camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the photographs be admitted, again, as a separate exhibit from Ms. Sutherland's bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes let's please call it 216. This leaves open 215 for the report provided by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then the photos, then they are tendered, 216-1 to -6. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no objections. Only I'm not sure whether we have the same set of photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Everyone should have the same set, although there's the extra Manjaca ones attached to it which I haven't put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll check it with your case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then admitted into evidence, S216-1 to -6. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you refer in your report to the Kozarac area, and also to coming across a convoy. Before I ask you on each aspect of that, did you see the convoy on your way to Trnopolje or on the way back, or Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I'm not certain, but I remember the convoy was travelling east on that main road which runs from -- which runs east towards Banja Luka, or southeast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, let's deal with that final part of your report that you made, which was headed: "Population movement." "While in the area, the team came across a convoy carrying an estimated 300 to 400 people moving from Sanski Most (an area with a large Muslim population) to Travnik (a Muslim-held area) presumably to be sent across the front line, either unilaterally or in exchange for Serb prisoners. Muslim and Croat refugees" -- it has been chopped off I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think that word is "also."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also continued to cross from northern Bosnia into Croatia. Does it read caveat?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can explain that now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: There has been a part of this report removed, I think one further paragraph whose heading was: "Caveat". I don't recall precisely what that said, but I'm reasonably confident that I said something like, treat this information with caution. We had a problem at one stage in the ECMM where our reports were not being acted on as we wished back in the European capitals. And there was one incident where the European presidency condemned the shelling of civilians outside Jajce in Bosnia. I was very surprised to see this because I knew the press had reported this shelling of civilians. And we checked very very carefully all our sources and we had no reliable report that civilians had been, in fact, shelled. And we had emphasised this in our reports, and still a public condemnation had been made of this unconfirmed report from some few people. And this made me angry because it reduced our credibility in the eyes of the Bosnian Serb leadership. It seemed to them sometimes as if they would be dammed if they did something bad, and they would be damned if they didn't. Now, I say this because I think it's relevant to my evidence. As a result of this, I put a caveat in to warn against -- I can't remember how I would have put it. But to make sure that this information was used correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, just before everybody thinks that the Prosecution has been removing things, this is how we acquired the document from ECMM. I hasten to add this is not an excision made by us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I can explain that, if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that the caveat was removed, I think, by the head of mission before he sent it out with his covering letter. So this is the version that he sent to the foreign office in London.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. Was this the only time during those two or three days that you were with Sir John that you saw one of these convoys of refugees?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I think Sir John may not have been in the vehicle with me when I saw this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, you refer to the team visiting part of Kozarac, which the Court knows would have been on your way back from Trnopolje through to Prijedor, that area. But what was the area like when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Can you just refer me to the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report on Trnopolje --

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: There we go, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You refer to the team visiting part of Kozarac and found nearly all the houses burnt.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. Now I can't recall whether I personally was in the team or part of a team that visited that part of Kozarac. I certainly saw houses near there myself. I was reporting here on behalf of the team, and it makes no difference, in my view, whether it was me personally or not. But the team, whether it included me or not, did go and visit those houses in Kozarac and described them in the same way that we had seen the houses lining the route and the houses that I had personally seen. And the striking thing was to any military person that there were no bullet marks in the walls and no shell splash marks visible, but the houses were burnt out. And when I asked what had happened, the reply was: "Well, there was a battle that's happened here." But no battle would cause that kind of visible evidence. I didn't pursue the matter at the time in discussion, but it was quite clear to us that while there may have been a few shells to frighten people, there had been no kind of military engagement, as I would understand it, other than perhaps some intimidation. So, it was a clear piece of evidence that we were not being told the truth about what had happened in Kozarac. And by implications other similar places in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's all I want to ask you about that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Your Honour, may that now be admitted as S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 215. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's clearly the document composed by the witness, so we don't have any objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, S215A and B respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, before I come to the report of the whole of Sir John's mission, may I ask you this: With Sir John, did you actually visit a particular enclave of Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where that was?
