utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: It was in a suburb of Prijedor or a village very close to Prijedor, but I think probably a suburb of Prijedor town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you talk to the residents there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. In quite a relaxed manner, for quite some time. Let's say an hour or more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything in particular about their houses?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, there were white flags hanging, jutting out from the front of all the houses or nearly all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should have asked you this: In respect of the burnt-out houses that you noticed on the route, were there also houses still standing?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. Normally, where there had been a large number of burnt-out houses, there would be some individual houses with their roofs and everything intact. And I think all of those houses, though there may have been some exceptions, had the Serbian mark on it of the cross with the four Cs, to show that that house belonged to a Serb family and should not be torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I want you to look, please, at the full report that was prepared as a result of Sir John Thomson's mission, which I hope --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have Your Honours got a copy of? It does have a 65 ter number. I can't think what it is. 354.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, just to make this clear, I think it's right, you had no hand in the actual writing of this report.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you read the report at or about the time that it was published?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I can't remember, but it would have been extremely likely that I read the report immediately after publication. We would have received a copy, and I was directly involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having gone through it, I think you're able to make various observations based on your part in this whole mission. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's headed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, because it's a very lengthy report, I'm going to read in full certain passages, but summarise others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's headed: "Report of the CSCE mission to inspect places of detention in Bosnia-Herzegovina, 29th of August, to the 4th of September 1992." And the first page, if we turn to that, is a summary of its recommendations, the first being that: "The CSCE to pronounce against the policy of ethnic cleansing and insist that it not provide a basis for future settlement of the dispute. 2: To insist on accountability of all authorities, parties, and individuals participating in the conflict. "3: CSCE to declare forcible disposal of property null and void. "4: CSCE to insist that all other prisoners be released immediately and in a safe and controlled manner. "5: CSCE to recommend the immediate evacuation of Trnopolje 'open centre'." And then I'm going to leave out the rest because they were effectively political recommendations, I think. Well, Item 9 urges -- encourage the ICRC urgently to devote resources to the process of identifying and monitoring detainees. So then if we go to the introduction, the first part explains how the terms of reference were developed, and then in paragraph 2: "This humanitarian mission was headed by Sir John Thomson of the United Kingdom who was assisted by ambassador Kenneth Blackwell of the United States and a distinguished group of international legal, medical, and political experts and a full list of the mission is attached at Appendix G." And then it says: "The main task of the mission was to survey the human rights situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina through direct observation of the detention camps and centres throughout the country insofar as it could in the one-week duration of the mission. The team saw places of detention where thousands are held, often under conditions of severe hardship and sometimes of terror. "The mission was also tasked to offer concrete proposals and to take appropriate steps during its operation which support fulfillment of the vital humanitarian tasks of the ICRC and UNHCR and other international and local bodies." And then it talks about how the leader, Sir John, attended the London Conference and talked with leaders of several of the factions so that the mission was thus able to set out with some assurance of local support. Nonetheless, it was apparent that the supposed support owed more to political than to humanitarian considerations. Then the method of work, and we can summarise this, I think. Is this right, Mr. Mayhew, effectively the mission was split into two?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. One team went south to, roughly speaking, the Muslim and Croat-held areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the other team covered the north areas of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And effectively we see the itinerary, and then the acknowledgments, one of which was to your organisation, the ECMM, and then the plan of the report. The next part deals with the background, and I think it's worth just reading a little bit of what was said. "The tragic story of the disintegration of the Yugoslav state and the outbreak of war and violence is well-known to the world community and needs no reiteration in this report. Yet, it would be wrong not to record that seasoned international observers who have witnessed many a conflict were impressed by the degree of bitterness involved. They heard that people who had lived comfortably together as neighbours for years suddenly denounced each other and enviously expropriated the property of the weaker group. There was much anecdotal evidence that mixed marriages were disrupted, and that in such cases, divorce was a common occurrence. The barbarism that occurred on a large scale, especially given the small size of the population of BH, some 4.4 million, was frequently inflicted by people who knew their victims. This is not an impersonal war. It is a civil war between communities for territorial expansion and ethnic supremacy. The first casualty has been good neighbourliness and compassion. The second, truth." Mr. Mayhew, did that, as it were, overall conclusion accord with your view of what had happened?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's very well put.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is then -- there's a further part which deals with how it should be approached, and then talks about the consequences of what has happened. "The virulent nationalistic wave that is now sweeping across the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. former Yugoslavia has produced death and destruction on a huge scale. Thousands of homes have been destroyed. An estimated 1.9 million people have become refugees or displaced persons." And then it talks about the economy and the history of the Balkans. Then if we go to Part I on page 5, effectively this is, again, a sort of summary of the aims and the limitations, I suppose, of this mission. "There is no doubt that massive violations of basic human rights have occurred in the former Yugoslavia. The evidence of refugee reports, press and television stories, and the credible statements of hundreds of eyewitnesses testify to anguish and tragedy to a degree that is almost unbearable for those who have seen it. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, once an impressive oasis of ethnic cooperation and cohabitation has been caught up in the Yugoslav madness and is now torn by savagery. The passions engaged in this once-peaceful republic have produced a situation in which the facts and the truth have become enmeshed in partisan distortion. And this is possibly an unduly gentle way of expressing the reality." That last part, Mr. Mayhew, again, how does that accord with your experience of what had happened in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Again, I think it's very well-put. I might have said something very similar myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, as I say, the next paragraph really deals with the limitations of the investigations that could be conducted, and indeed, at the end of that -- before we get to the detention and notification part, they say that this report -- "the problems preclude any claim that this report is the last word on the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It should be viewed as the first in a series." And then it talks about the detention and notification and pays tribute to Mr. Mazowiecki and the ICRC and UNHCR. Over to page 6, please. There it lists how many places ICRC had visited and talks about the difficulty in notification of places of detention. In the middle of the paragraph it says: "In the reports which were available to us, it is clear that Serb forces in BH hold a disproportionate share of the prisoners. We can make no claim to know with indisputable accuracy the number of prisoners and hostages held by all sides." And it then goes on to talk about reports of private prisoners, areas where villages were effectively turned into a detention camp. And then explains how it came to visit the various places that it did. If we go over to page 7: "Mr. Karadzic, the Bosnian Serb leader, explained to the mission that Pale, the seat of his authority, had no camps or centres of detention. However, at approximately the same time, his officials were notifying the ICRC of 50 prisoners in Pale. This is at least a fault in the preferable direction. In our opinion, it is more common for places of detention to be denied. The authorities tend to deceive themselves into supposing that the truth is whatever they say it is." And then it goes on to talk about the international community insisting on notification. Then: "Lack of respect for civilian population. The mission determined that a complete range of individuals, both male and females, young and old, are now being held throughout BH in various places of detention. We met with prisoners as young as 17, or even less, and as old as 83. The crucial point is that thousands are being held against their will or under conditions which make their departure from the places of their confinement virtually impossible." From your own observations, Mr. Mayhew, it says "as young as 17 or less and as old as 83," were you able to establish those sort of ages from the people you were able to talk to?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I didn't ask people their exact ages. It is credible to me that -- there were certainly some elderly around, and it's credible to me that that very old age is possible. It's also credible to me, particularly credible, that people of 17 or younger, providing they looked as if they were males of fighting age would be held. The aim was not to draw a line at an age limit; the aim was to reduce the threat to the detainer, the detainer's community, and anyone aged 15, 16, who looked as if they would fight, once sent to the other side, would be eligible for detention. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did you get the impression that they were detaining anybody who looked as though they could be of fighting age?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: In looking in Trnopolje and Manjaca, the majority were of fighting age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then they go on in the report to deal with the types, the categories of prisoners. First, prisoners of war. "These prisoners have taken an active part in hostilities and can legally be detained." "The mission saw very few of these. It was our impression that much of the fighting was to the death." Leaving aside the second part of that, would you agree that you saw very few people who actually appeared to have taken part -- in an active part in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, that was our impression. Of course, everyone was in civilian clothes and so would not necessarily look any different. So my impression is partly from general knowledge of the situation and partly from the stories taken, at random with no notice in snatches, from the men who were there. And they gave me every indication of having -- of telling the truth and of having really no idea why they were there. And they all said about everyone that they were civilians. We learned increasingly to distinguish between -- to try to distinguish between people who were lying to us and people who were telling the truth. There is a great deal of falsehood in what is said. In our meetings, particularly with leaders, it has entered part of I'm afraid to say managing a crisis, perhaps more widely than that, but I've only know this area during wartime or crisis. So we had to develop a sense of feel as to when we were being led astray and when we were being spoken to truthfully. Now, I do not claim that I knew infallibly when I was being lied to, but I simply rested on my experience of a few months in the region and a general feel for what is military and what isn't, based on my previous professional experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, just to interrupt, at the record we can read that the paragraph you just read out on prisoners of war, it was there cited as a quotation, but when it is a quotation, it has to be added that it reads "they can legally be detained as combatants under the 3rd Geneva Convention of 1949."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I left out the words. I said legally detained, but left out the -- Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're on that topic, Mr. Mayhew, just to the Court understands, after your experience in Bosnia, did you in fact go and work in Rwanda?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, and thereafter, I think it was the Congo?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now, at this stage, you've had quite a lot of experience in dealing with...

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, I spent a year in Rwanda immediately following the genocide and war and two years in the Congo during the two wars there, as a UN manager and as an NGO humanitarian manager, respectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look at the second category B. "People who had allegedly been hiding weapons in their homes and/or possessed information of potential military significance. Their civilian (noncombatant) status should have protected them from military detention although they could arguably be subject to judicial proceedings. There were probably a significant number of those." And then category C: "People who were taken prisoner because they lived or worked in the zone of combat. These people were not taking part in hostilities, but were seen as enemies due to their ethnic origin. Their civilian (noncombatant) status should have protected them from detention. This category was easily the largest. "Our experience suggests that a comparatively small percentage of prisoners are genuine POWs. The remainder should never have been imprisoned. We are not impressed by claims that they were incarcerated for their own safety or simply because they happened to be resident in a combat zone. It is impossible to escape the conclusion that most prisoners are innocent people who have been seized as hostages to promote "ethnic cleansing." They are pawns in vicious games played by nationalist politicians. These innocent people should be released forthwith." Again, Mr. Mayhew, does that paragraph -- first of all, paragraph C, the third category was the largest, would you agree from your observations that seemed to be right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. And I think I mentioned in the Manjaca report that the definition of "prisoner of war" seemed often to be someone who was arrested within a combat zone; simply that. And this seemed to be the definition that we received when we posed the question to camp authorities, and we were very surprised that the definition should be simply that, without any attempt to add something on to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the conclusion or the observation that "most prisoners are innocent people, seized as hostages to promote ethnic cleansing" would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, I would guess that a proportion of them, a minority, would have felt quite ready to pick up a weapon, if available, and either defend themselves or take part in offensive operations. After all, they would feel a loyalty to their own community. But my impression was that the great majority had had no opportunity to do that, and therefore would not have done that. And therefore, were not correctly arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph deals with a phenomenon I don't think you saw, where a whole village had been turned into a camp effectively.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the paragraph after that: "The frequent and deliberate destruction of dwellings of the local population (of one or the other ethnic group) can never be justified as an action against military targets, a claim that was made to the mission. The ethnically selective torching of houses constitutes, in all circumstances, a grave violation of international humanitarian law, and military commanders or political authorities who were in a position to prevent such acts should be held legally responsible for them." Then the report goes on to discuss the dilemma of the assessment of these prisoners, and the groups who are participating in the conflict. And perhaps I should read the second part of this paragraph. "There are all sorts of uniformed and nonuniformed armed groups and units participating in the conflict. Some are the creation of what can only be understood as local warlords; others represent some kind of community defence force; and still others are the armed part of a right-wing political party. Moreover, individuals have been mobilised directly from their homes and fight in civilian clothes. "All authorities told us that the prisoners they held were legitimate prisoners of war." Pausing there, Mr. Mayhew, that goes back to what you just told us, that that was their definition of prisoners of war. "Serb authorities also insisted that they had the right to hold "individuals taken in the area of the conflict." And again, pausing, Mr. Mayhew, is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Of course, it occurs to me now that if our impressions about Kozarac, for example, are accurate, the term doesn't even apply because it was not an area of conflict that they had taken, if there was no battle in somewhere like Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it talks about international legal experts, and then goes on to say: "Moreover, in our discussions with hundreds of detainees in Serb, Muslim, and Croat places of detention, we found an appalling number of individuals who we believe are, in fact, civilians with little, if any, direct connection with the conflict. We are also very disturbed by the assertions from the parties that many of the people they hold under these severe conditions are being held for their own "protection." Serb authorities in Prijedor, for example, insisted that they were protecting the Muslims from Muslim "extremists" who were fighting a guerilla campaign from the former partisan stronghold of Korazde mountain. "We urge that a renewed effort be made to identify clearly those innocent civilians now being held and steps be taken forthwith to secure their immediate release and adequate protection after their release." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Then it talks about what you've mentioned, the approach of winter. And then the responsibility of leaders. "Despite the existence of 'warlords' the bulk of the evidence points to the responsibility of acknowledged leaders. The mission believes that in general, leaders exchange effective control over their military and civilian structures. Contrary to what is usually accepted, the so-called "uncontrolled elements" are marginal. They exist, but their importance has been exaggerated by various leaders who find them a convenient explanation for numerous barbarities. The mission have seen camps well-organised with military personnel or policemen doing what they were told to do." Now, again, Mr. Mayhew, that paragraph, how does that accord with your knowledge or impressions of what had been happening?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Very well. So far, from -- in northern Bosnia, the leaders hardly ever, if ever, said that some areas were out of their control in areas which they claimed to be the authorities of. And this is understandable, because one of their main political aims at the time was to convince us and the outside world that they were about to become a nation or something close to a nation, sovereign, and needed to be convincing that they had proper power and authority. And we never came across any evidence that local warlords were operating in northern Bosnia with an effective autonomous area. There may have been more cause for claiming that in southwestern Bosnia where forces were much more irregular and newly created. But in northern Bosnia, I don't recall any example of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the sentence that "camps well organised...," you would agree that you saw as well?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, there was firm, clear organisation and chains of command evident -- particularly at Manjaca, and also at Trnopolje. It was clear that the uniformed personnel were under clear command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it -- the rest of the paragraph, I don't propose to read, because it deals with the agreements that had been signed. Over the page, it continues: "However, the mission is very conscious that on all sides, there have been numerous breaches of the Geneva Conventions, and that to a significant extent, some of these continue. The most widespread breach by all parties is the long continued detention, in some cases of more than three months, of civilians who cannot possibly be classified as prisoners of war. The largest number of these appear to be in Serb places of detention; and therefore, while the international community should bear down heavily on all parties, it should do so particularly firmly on the Serbs." Then: "The lack of transparency. The mission is very concerned about the lack of transparency in relation to prisoners. The leaders and the people we met work very much along the lines of the old communist system of suspicion and opacity. This opacity perpetuates bitterness and leads to a situation in which virtually all stories about atrocities are believed. Naturally, it has its effect inside the camps as well as outside them. Thus nothing is readily verifiable except the terror to be observed in the eyes of the prisoners." So again, Mr. Mayhew, the report is echoing what you told us about your earlier experience when you were in the Banja Luka area in April.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, it's well and fairly written.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it deals with there are going to be suggestions made. And then it goes on: "The ethnic cleansing operations which are taking place with official connivance or direct support have left people virtually defenceless even in their own homes. Murders, rapes, robberies, assaults, and beatings are continuing. Those who carry out these activities are often personally known by their victims and by others in the community. Few have reportedly been brought to justice." That information, Mr. Mayhew, in this report would have come from who?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think it would have come from -- partly from prisoners, and partly from people like myself who were interlocutors with the mission, and partly from other people who they met during their mission. And they may have spoken to people en route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And then the next paragraph: "Local authorities who profess to be powerless to prevent such abuses and who claim lack of knowledge cannot be allowed to continue" --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We don't hear the French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Nothing can be heard in French, indeed. Yes, I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just add something to my previous response.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Mayhew, yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think that the ICRC was obviously another important source of information on the question you posed just before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I stopped. I'll just read again the part of that next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Local authorities who profess to be powerless to prevent such abuses and who claim lack of knowledge should not be allowed to continue such charades." Again, Mr. Mayhew, how do you view that statement?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: It is perfectly possibly that there were a number of isolated incidents which realistically the authorities could do little or nothing about. However, the general situation was one of effective control throughout their areas of governance. And I agree with the sentence here for that reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the remainder of the paragraph deals with the dangers of effectively closing the camps and pushing them out. And then they record their view of Trnopolje. "We would like to call the chairman's attention to the Trnopolje so-called open centre in the Serb-conquered area around Prijedor. This dismissal location no longer has barbed wire surrounding it, and Serb officials insisted that the inmates were free to come and go as they pleased. Our interviews with the persons within that facility produced a vastly different perspective. Most of the 2.000 or so Muslims were civilians driven from their homes in the region by Serb forces. Their residences have been burnt, bombed, or occupied by immigrant Serb families, leaving them no local place to go to should they wish to do so. Numbers of detainees who have left the camp have never returned; and when night falls, the level of personal security reportedly drops precipitously. We discussed this situation with controlling political authorities; and as a result, have developed a plan of action which is set out in Part II." Now, two matters, Mr. Mayhew: The reference to "detainees who have left the camp not returning," was that something that you heard about, or other members of the mission?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Other members of the mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the level of personal security dropping at night?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: That specific detail I didn't hear; however, it accords with my overall impression that they were frightened, not feeling secure at that moment in that camp. And so that daily experience was clearly one of insecurity and fear, and it was the kind of fear consistent with the fear of being shot or beaten when people are not looking. But no one said to me, as far as I recall, except where I may have recorded that in a report, that people had been -- that people had been shot. I think I may have said that in a Trnopolje report in which case, that will be accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then were you a party to any discussion with the political authorities about this after the visit?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I attended the meetings that the mission had, and I don't recall whether there was a meeting with the authorities after the -- outside the camp after the visit to Trnopolje. But if there was, I would have been present. They may be referring -- no, they obviously are not referring to camp authorities present on the ground, unless they were accompanied by political authorities at that camp visit in which case that may be the discussion that they are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the next paragraph: "Treatment of prisoners by authorities. With very few exceptions, camp authorities have little sympathy for detainees. We witnessed the results of beatings, wounds, fractures, and other injuries in camps controlled by Serbian, Muslim, and Croatian authorities, and have reason to believe that innocent prisoners on all sides have been executed. The prisoners interviewed are reluctant in most cases to provide specific detail concerning atrocities, but many provided hints. We conclude that some camp authorities have treated the detainees with relative fairness, given the current circumstances, whilst others have been clearly abusive or at least have tolerated mistreatment of detainees." Now, did you see any signs in Trnopolje yourself of beatings or other injuries?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen anything of that nature in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Again, I don't think so, though there were people in the medical centre with a variety of complaints including injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it goes on to talk about the conditions and describes the type of accommodation that there was. Then it effectively talks about overcrowding, about water and food and then sanitation and hygiene. And then "health of prisoners. While many civilians in BH are said to be short of nutritious food, there can be no doubt that a majority of prisoners are more seriously deprived." And then effectively the concentration is on Manjaca. Mr. Mayhew, would you agree that from what you saw, that was the worst?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: That Manjaca was the worst?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the malnutrition that was seen.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: In terms of malnutrition, yes, and we were always conscious that here was a camp on display, on show, this is the stage that it had reached after being prepared to be shown to the outside world with notice given and so on. So anyone -- what we were seeing was the best, and that anyone in a worse state, and it is reasonable to estimate that there would have been some, would have not been shown to us, would have been spirited away. And this was after some months as well. So we were I think quite reasonably deducing, by implication, that previous conditions had been significantly worse than what we were seeing, but of course we didn't report that because we hadn't seen it. But I think it's a reasonable deduction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the report talks about interviews with prisoners, and again talks about the fear that they experienced and the behaviour that you've already described, of how they walked and the like in Manjaca. And then again, medical services, physical work outside the centre, and then the visits by the ICRC and family visits. And then finally, it talks about violations of international humanitarian law and really deals with the legal consequences according to the report's writers. While we're on that subject, having read this report again, reminding yourself, who would have been responsible for this report, effectively?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Sir John Thomson. Well his whole team would have had responsibility individually for the report because they all agreed it. It strikes me that this is written by him directly, or at least with significant editing by him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we come to the recommendations, and again, I'm going to summarise this. What seems to have been concerning the mission most was the approaching winter. Would you agree, Mr. Mayhew, that was a problem?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. One of the major problems. I recall -- and I'd like to add one thing about the conditions on water supply. You showed me the photograph. Thinking about that a little more, it was clear from the hygiene conditions and the medical condition of prisoners found in the medical centre, and the number of complaints of diarrhea and so on, that the water supply was well below what was needed. And it is difficult to argue that water was in such short supply that the authorities couldn't afford to give more water. There is plenty of water. It requires fuel to get it there, but it's not really the same argument that one could use for food. And in that culture, high levels of water supply for basic washing and for health and hygiene are really required. So I wanted to make sure that that was noted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure that we need go through really the recommendations because I think effectively we dealt with the summary of them in the beginning of the report. If we then skip the map, there is then a list of the alleged places of detention, based on lists supplied. We see the first part deals with alleged concentration camps for Serbs in Bosnia. Then the next, page 21, prisons in Sarajevo with Serbs in them. A lot of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those. And then if we go to page 23, we see the following list was received from the mayor of Banja Luka. And again, that's alleged places of detention holding Serbs. And then if we go to page 25, there's a special memorandum there on Trnopolje, yes, which talks about special arrangements that should relate to it, the reason being given: "The number of inmates at the centre, of whom the great majority, if not all, are of the Muslim faith, is currently thought to be in the neighbourhood of 2.000. These people are living in terror, and the CSCE mission believe they have substantial reasons for their fears." And it then makes recommendations about teams to go in and register and deal with food deficiencies and the like. And in fact, effectively try and close the camp down. Then there's the agreement that takes place in Geneva in May. And then if we go to page 32, we see the places of detention, actual and alleged, which were inspected during the mission. The first two, Bihac -- you didn't visit either Bihac or Ripac, did you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we see number 3, what I take should be the "Manjaca" as opposed to "Menjaca centre." And 3.000-odd detainees, Serbian, Muslim, 1.800, and then the list of other places visited. And then there is a further description of each of the places that were visited during the course of the mission. And I rather think that, yes, there's yet another description of Trnopolje at page 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Due to the fact that I believe it could be necessary to read this out in toto, we should have a break now, bringing us to 5 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. For the record, we can see Mr. Koumjian appearing for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There is one matter I wanted to address the Court regarding -- It regards the witness who Your Honours indicated yesterday you prefer to hear live. I believe it's number 47, 27. 27, excuse me. 27. We contacted that witness today, and just within the last half hour, the witness was able to confirm that the witness could come Sunday and testify on Monday, and the witness we were going to have on Monday would then testify on Tuesday. However, we were told by the VWU that there is a rule that they have that they must have five days' notice to arrange the trip of the witness. I don't want to be in the habit of asking the Court to make orders to the registry that has been so helpful to us so often. But in this particular case, especially at this time when no one is there to speak to, I would ask the Court if the Court could make an order or a request to the registry or the VWU on this particular occasion to help us bring the witness on Sunday. The witness is willing to come. There was a big potential next week that we wouldn't have enough witnesses to fill the time. I think it would be very, very convenient coming to the end of the trial. And in the end we're going to have a lot of witnesses trying to fit into a short space. So the fact that next week is an opportunity to hear a witness whose testimony will be very pertinent, we just have to arrange to bring him on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the reasons given by the OTP, the Trial Chamber requests the registry kindly to provide for the necessary, enabling the OTP to, and the Chamber and the parties, to hear Witness 27 already by Monday next week as time is of the essence. Thank you. I think this would be enough. If necessary, the Registrar himself in person should be contacted immediately. Let me know. I know he is still in the premises, and it's possible to contact him in person. If there is any obstacle I will help out --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I will go down right now to the VWU and try and work it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us know. Just to be on the safe side, I think, as I have seen no objections by the Defence to this procedure, and the necessary documents were provided already earlier to the Defence, this shouldn't be any obstacle for proceeding this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, I'm sorry about that small administrative interruption. Can we now look at the part of the report that describes the camps in rather more detail for Trnopolje, at page 47. Gives the location, then the facility: "This place of detention is in and around a two-storey structure formerly used as a school." Pausing there, can I take it that was the photograph we saw of that building?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It goes on: "The fencing was recently removed, and the periphery is irregularly patrolled by a uniformed authority armed with automatic rifles. A number of detainees are housed in the school, but a large number are sheltered in makeshift tents produced from scraps of wood and wire fencing covered with pieces of cloth or other material with little waterproofing in evidence. A number have made an empty truck their home in detention." Then: "Number of detainees and description: We have estimated 1600 to 2.000 Muslim males are quartered in this centre. They range in age from teenagers to 60 years or older, and virtually all are believed to be victims of ethnic cleansing, arrested in their homes in nearby towns and villages. Some have been relocated to the centre more recently after having experienced the horrors of the Omarska Detention Centre which was very recently closed. With a few exceptions, their families have been removed from the area, and their homes destroyed or occupied by Serbs." "Period of detention: A majority has been held in this centre for two to three months, whereas a smaller number has been moved here more recently from other places of detention in the area. "General conditions in Trnopolje: We have been led to believe that the authority is relatively relaxed during the mornings and until 3.00 p.m. each afternoon, when the major in charge completes his onsite duties. Until that time, the detainees are permitted to leave the centre to purchase (a minority) or scrounge for food without fear of reprisal. However, after dusk, the unsupervised guards often harass and mistreat the detainees with no apparent provocation. Beatings are apparently common, and there is good reason to believe that some detainees are removed and executed, or at least never to be seen nor heard from again. This centre appears to have no real organisation and it undoubtedly `a disaster ready to happen'. "Health-related conditions: Water for consumption and washing of self and clothing is brought to the centre in a tanker truck most days and remains while the detainees fill whatever containers they have available, plastic bottles, pots, and pans, et cetera. It is impossible to maintain personal hygiene under such circumstances. The two-person pit latrine is not maintained and is completely contrary to basic accepted norms. The grounds are relatively free of litter, but the single waste container was overflowing on to the surrounding mud courtyard. There was an extensive waste disposal area in one corner of the camp which was also used as a latrine. "Even though no meals are provided by the authority, there is less evidence of malnourished detainees in this centre than in most other places of detention. They have been permitted to leave the centre to search for food, and relatives or friends have brought in what food they could spare. During the past week or so, the ICRC has delivered prepared meals, one for each detainee. Several detainees are seriously malnourished. They were usually persons who have arrived recently from Omarska or other more inhumane places of detention. "We were unable to assess accurately the general physical health of detainees, but the fact that they live out of doors in a gypsy-like existence has probably been to their advantage and will continue to be so until the colder and damper weather arrives several weeks hence. At that time, these individuals will be placed at particularly great risk. "There is obvious evidence to suggest that detainees in the centre, as in other locations, have been subjected to terrible psychic stress prior to and during incarceration. However, they have maintained some contact with the outside world, which appears to have provided a protective effect. There can be no doubt that they share most of the fears and uncertainties of detainees in Manjaca and other centres, but they walk about the centre relatively freely, play chess and engage in more lively conversations with their fellows. "A medical clinic has been set up in one of the school rooms, staffed by two medical students who appear to be relatively sensitive to clients' concerns. They have very little to offer in treatment since the supply of drugs and other materials is very limited. Seriously ill or injured have been transferred to a local hospital, but very infrequently, as it appears. "To your knowledge, detainees here are not frequently permitted to work except to keep the grounds neat and tidy, but there is currently unlimited opportunity to remain out of doors in the sunshine. "ICRC and other assistance: The ICRC has been able to visit Trnopolje during the past two or three weeks and has documented detainee details in addition to arranging for the delivery of preprepared meals. Relatives and friends are permitted to visit freely, at least during daytime hours. We were told that bread is delivered to the camp periodically by the local Red Cross, who sometimes charge detainees who may be able to pay." And then it deals with the notes. The visit was on the 31st of August. Next part of the report dealt with Manjaca, and then the other places of detention visited. And finally, we see at the back the list of the people who were members of the mission. Finally on this report, Mr. Mayhew, you told us the mission had split. Sir John Thomson went on your part of the mission. Do you know who else on this list went?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I recall that someone who was acting as a local advisor -- or advisor on the local area and who spoke the local language was on the team, and I imagine that that was Mr. Davico who is at the bottom of that list. As for the others, I'm not certain which of them was on my section of the team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's right. You knew Mr. Telle, the --

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Telle, I met him in several crises and I can't be certain that I actually met him on this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask that this report be admitted as S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it possible for us to reserve our right after cross-examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Then this document has provisionally the number 217, and we wait until the end of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the mission was completed, Mr. Mayhew, I think you told us you went back again, escorting somebody else to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was a man called Dr. Gilbert Greenhalgh [phoen] who was sent by the British government, I think possibly under the umbrella also of the European Community presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thereafter, did you return to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, and I can deal with this quite shortly because again, it's more in connection with Manjaca, did you assist in the evacuation of some 69 sick Muslims from the camp in Manjaca, the main organisers being the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. Were they all from Manjaca, the report will remind me. It occurs to me they might also have come from local hospitals, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely -- in fact it doesn't make it clear. There was an airlift, I think, from Banja Luka. I'm just going to see. Yes, well perhaps -- I'm going to ask for it to be exhibited, Your Honour. But it may help for Mr. Mayhew to refresh his memory. Could we show him from the 15th of September, attachment 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look -- this is what your normal daily summary report, is it, Mr. Mayhew, as you described, different from the --

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this is slightly different from what I described. This is from the regional centre, Sarajevo, as you see on the top right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: And that at this point was a cell within the headquarters in Zagreb. It's misleading, because we had no permanent people in Bosnia anymore. But the regional centre Sarajevo existed outside with the hope of going back in. But it retained that name, and it was the daily summary produced by me as the person responsible for that cell out of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And if we just look at the paragraph number 5: "Humanitarian issues. The delayed ICRC-sponsored airlift of 69 sick Muslims was successfully completed today. Three ECMM teams monitored the operation, although they took no direct part, the ICRC made it clear they were very grateful. Convoys brought the evacuees from Manjaca military prison camp, Trnopolje Open Reception Centre, and Banja Luka hospital to Banja Luka airport, and a chartered Aeroflot aircraft flew them out at 1540. It is hoped that this will kick start a much greater tide of evacuation of people who have lost their homes and are under threat as much from the winter as from the security situation. "Other matters: While delayed in Banja Luka for three days, an ECMM team met the three main religious leaders. All three were keen that the ECMM should redeploy permanently to the area and do anything possible to improve the situation which had worsened after the ECMM left the area in April. The team also met General Mladic, who reiterated many familiar views and demands, but was noticeably positive about the proposed return of the ECMM. The date of the ECMM next visit is not known. I depends on a higher level political agreement." So Mr. Mayhew, you're quite right, it was a mixture of people from various areas that were air-lifted out. And here we see the reference to General Mladic that you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, it's my fault, I think it should be made an exhibit, because it does refer to Trnopolje as well. And I've read it out now. So if there's no objection, could it be made S218.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted, S218.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, can I ask that you look at your report for the 26th of September, which was attachment 3. And before we deal with that, can I just note on that in passing, Mr. Mayhew, were you provided with a letter of thanks from the ICRC which had gone via the head of mission?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For your help in the airlift. Again, report from your daily summary: "General situation, one, political situation, NTR." Nothing to report. "B, military and operational situation: Dr. Karadzic last night refused permission by telephone for the ECMM to redeploy to Banja Luka or other Serb-held areas of BH. His reason was that local Muslims are waiting for the ECMM to return so that they can cause chaos and an uprising. ECMM redeployment would, therefore, worsen things." And I don't think the next is relevant. Did you ever get back to the area of northern Bosnia before you left?

utterances.speaker: JAMES MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't actually remember. Our main -- my job for the remainder of my time until March 1993 was the Bosnia desk officer, otherwise known as the person running the Sarajevo cell. And our big aim was to get teams back into all three areas of Bosnia, and we succeeded in the Muslim and Croat-held areas. But by the time I left, we had no permanent presence in the Bosnian Serb-held areas which was a matter of great regret to me. And of course it caused an unfortunate imbalance in our reporting, and we tried many times to be allowed back in without success. I don't remember a specific visit that I made. So it is possible that I didn't visit again, but I would be corrected by the reports. There will be reports if I visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be made Exhibit S219..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections. S219 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, that's all I ask of Mr. Mayhew. Mr. Mayhew, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the cross-examination? The Defence is prepared to start, at least to start today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if possible, we would like to start tomorrow because Mr. Ostojic should be here and to conduct that cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to say, Your Honour, "he hopes." Your Honour, certainly there's no objection. Mr. Mayhew is perfectly all right for tomorrow. It would be difficult if it went into Friday for him. But for tomorrow, he's available, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have to thank you for today. And you understood from that what has been said, it will be necessary to have some additional questions by the Defence, and probably also by the Judges tomorrow. But I'm convinced - convinced - that we can finalise your testimony by tomorrow. And if there is nothing additional to be said --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a matter I want to raise about the handwriting, but I think I'll raise it tomorrow because I'm still not all together clear from Mr. Koumjian what it is we're supposed to be raising. I better check that with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. I think all parties agree that it is time for finalising our today's hearing. The trial stands adjourned until tomorrow, 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
